species_smell.smell: Female trees produce seeds with a strong, unpleasant rancid odor, especially when fallen and crushed.
Young foliage contains aromatic oils and can give off a noticeable fresh, aromatic scent.
No strong or distinctive scent is generally associated with the flowers or foliage; any odor is usually subtle.
Flowers are lightly to moderately fragrant, with a delicate sweet floral scent; fragrance varies among trees and cultivars.
Foliage has a mild resinous or green conifer-like odor when crushed, but the tree is not generally known for a strong ambient fragrance.
Creamy-white flowers are distinctly fragrant, producing a noticeable sweet floral scent.
Flowers can have a noticeable sweet floral fragrance, although intensity varies.
Most flowers have little to no strong fragrance; some cultivars can have a faint, delicate floral scent.
Needles have a clear pine-like, fresh, resinous and slightly herbaceous aroma.
Flowers are fragrant; studies identify phenylethyl alcohol and other volatile compounds as important components of the floral scent.
Varies by species. The source groups multiple species under 'other', so there is no single representative smell.

notes.interpretation: Descriptions are general species-level scent characteristics and can vary by cultivar, sex, season, weather, and whether plant material is disturbed.
notes.data_limitation: The source statistics provide district-level species counts, not individual-tree scent observations.

sources.reference: University of Minnesota Campus Trees; Journal of Integrative Agriculture
Yu et al., 2004, Flavour and Fragrance Journal
Song & Hong, 2020, Journal of Asia-Pacific Biodiversity
